questions.question: The Chinese traveler who visited Harsha's court was:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hiuen Tsang**__.

• **Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang)** was a Chinese Buddhist monk, scholar, and traveler who visited India during King Harsha's reign (606–647 CE).
 
• He arrived in India around **631 CE** and spent over 15 years studying Indian culture, religion, and philosophy.
 
• Hiuen Tsang documented his travels in the renowned text **"Si-Yu-Ki" (Records of the Western Regions)**, which offers valuable insights into Indian society during Harsha's era.
 
• He visited Harsha's court at Kannauj and was warmly received by the king, who organized debates and discussions on Buddhist philosophy.
 
• Hiuen Tsang's accounts provide detailed descriptions of cities, universities like Nalanda, political administration, and the socio-economic conditions in India during the 7th century.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fa-Hien**

 
 
• Fa-Hien was another Chinese traveler who visited India earlier (399–414 CE) during the Gupta period.
 
• He primarily focused on Buddhist texts and monastic practices and documented his travels in "A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms."
 
 
 
• **I-Tsing**
 
 
• I-Tsing was a Chinese Buddhist monk and traveler who visited India in the 7th century, primarily to study Buddhism at Nalanda University.
 
• He wrote extensively about Buddhist practices and translated several Indian texts into Chinese.
 
 
 
• **King Harsha**
 
 
• Harsha was a ruler of northern India known for his patronage of Buddhism and other religions.
 
• Under his rule, Kannauj became a center of learning and culture.

questions.question: British land revenue policies were deeply exploitative. Under which system were landlords required to pay a fixed revenue regardless of crop yield?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Zamindari**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Zamindari system was introduced by the British East India Company in 1793 through the **Permanent Settlement Act** in parts of Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha.
 
• Under this system, Zamindars (landlords) were made the owners of the land and were tasked to collect a fixed revenue from the peasants.
 
• The Zamindars had to pay a fixed amount of revenue to the British government, irrespective of the actual agricultural output or crop yield.
 
• Failure to pay the fixed revenue would result in the confiscation of the Zamindar's land by the British authorities.
 
• This system was highly exploitative, as Zamindars often extracted exorbitant rents from the farmers, leading to widespread poverty and distress among the peasantry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Permanent Settlement Act (1793):**

 
 
• Introduced by Lord Cornwallis, it aimed to create a loyal class of landlords who would support British rule.
 
• Zamindars were recognized as the hereditary owners of the land, with the right to collect rent from peasants.
 
• The land revenue was fixed permanently, meaning it would not be increased in the future.
 
 
 
• **Ryotwari System:**
 
 
• Introduced in Madras and Bombay Presidencies by Thomas Munro and Alexander Read.
 
• Under this system, peasants (ryots) were recognized as the landowners and were directly responsible for paying land revenue to the government.
 
 
 
• **Mahalwari System:**
 
 
• Implemented in parts of North-Western Provinces, Punjab, and Central India.
 
• Revenue settlement was made collectively with a village or group of villages (mahal).
 
 
 
• **Exploitation Under Zamindari:**
 
 
• The fixed revenue often exceeded the peasant's capacity to pay, especially during famines or crop failures.
 
• The system resulted in the marginalization of peasants and the enrichment of Zamindars.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 11**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 11** of the Indian Constitution empowers the Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship through legislation.
 
• It allows the Parliament to make laws concerning the acquisition, termination, and other matters related to citizenship.
 
• This article is part of Part II (Articles 5 to 11) of the Constitution, which deals with Citizenship.
 
• Using the powers under Article 11, the Parliament has enacted laws like the **Citizenship Act of 1955** and its subsequent amendments.
 
• While Articles 5 to 10 determine the citizenship status of individuals at the commencement of the Constitution, Article 11 enables future legislative actions on citizenship matters.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Part II of the Constitution:** It deals with the provisions related to citizenship from Articles 5 to 11.
 
• **Citizenship Act of 1955:** This law, enacted under Article 11, specifies the methods for acquiring, losing, and determining Indian citizenship.
 
• **Modes of Acquiring Citizenship:** The Citizenship Act provides five modes: by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory.
 
• **Amendments to Citizenship Act:** Significant amendments include the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, which introduced provisions for granting citizenship to certain persecuted minorities from neighboring countries.
 
• **Difference Between Articles 5-10 and Article 11:** Articles 5-10 primarily address citizenship at the time of the Constitution's commencement, while Article 11 grants the Parliament the power to legislate on citizenship matters post-constitution.

questions.question: Which of the following caves contain rock cut paintings dating back to the stone age era?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bhimbetka Caves**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Bhimbetka Caves are a UNESCO World Heritage Site located in the Raisen district of Madhya Pradesh, India.
 
• The rock shelters of Bhimbetka contain paintings that date back to the Stone Age, specifically the Mesolithic period (c. 10,000 BCE).
 
• These paintings depict scenes from everyday life, including hunting, dancing, and communal activities, providing insights into the lives of early humans.
 
• The art includes representations of animals such as bison, tigers, and elephants, as well as human figures engaged in activities.
 
• The Bhimbetka Cave complex is one of the earliest examples of human interaction with the environment, showcasing continuity in artistic expression over thousands of years.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rock Art Terminology:**

 
 
• Rock art refers to human-made markings placed on natural stone, typically in caves or open-air shelters.
 
• It includes petroglyphs (carvings) and pictographs (paintings).
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Status:**
 
 
• Bhimbetka was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003 due to its archaeological and cultural significance.
 
• The site is noted for its unique record of human settlement and evolution over different historical periods.
 
 
 
• **Mesolithic Period:**
 
 
• The Mesolithic period, also known as the Middle Stone Age, is characterized by the transition from hunting and gathering to agriculture.
 
• Rock art from this period is significant for its depiction of social and cultural development.
 
 
 
• **Discovery of Bhimbetka:**
 
 
• The caves were first discovered by Indian archaeologist V.S. Wakankar in 1957 while surveying the Narmada Valley.
 
• Over 750 rock shelters have been identified, with around 500 containing paintings.
 
 
 
• **Comparative Sites:**
 
 
• Other significant rock art sites in India include the Adamgarh Hills (Madhya Pradesh) and the Kupgal petroglyphs (Karnataka).
 
• Globally, comparable sites include the Lascaux Caves in France and the Altamira Cave in Spain.

• The Kanva Dynasty ruled for approximately 45 years, with four rulers: Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, and Susharman.
 
• The Kanvas were eventually overthrown by the Satavahanas, who expanded their influence in the Deccan and northern India.
 
• The Kanva Dynasty is considered a transitional period in Indian history, marked by political instability and regional fragmentation.

• The Shungas ruled Magadha from approximately 185 BCE to 73 BCE, succeeding the Mauryan Empire.
 
• They were known for their patronage of art, including the construction of the Bharhut and Sanchi Stupas.
 
• The dynasty was marked by internal rebellions and external threats, leading to its eventual decline.
 
 
 
• **Satavahana Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Satavahanas succeeded the Kanva Dynasty and ruled large parts of central and southern India.
 
• They were known for their contributions to trade, art, and architecture, including the Amaravati Stupa.

• The Kanva Dynasty faced challenges in maintaining control over Magadha due to its brief rule and external invasions.

questions.question: Which of the following materials is most suitable for making filaments in electric bulbs?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tungsten**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tungsten** is the most suitable material for making electric bulb filaments due to its **high melting point** of approximately 3422°C, which allows it to operate at high temperatures without melting.
 
• It has a very low rate of evaporation at high temperatures, ensuring a longer lifespan of the filament.
 
• Tungsten has excellent tensile strength, which prevents it from breaking easily when subjected to thermal expansion and contraction.
 
• Its high resistivity enables it to convert electrical energy into heat efficiently, producing bright light.
 
• When used in an inert gas-filled bulb, tungsten's performance is further enhanced by reducing filament evaporation and improving efficiency.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Properties of Tungsten:**

 
 
• The high melting point of tungsten makes it suitable for applications requiring heat resistance.
 
• Its density is around 19.3 g/cm³, making it one of the heaviest metals.
 
• Tungsten's low vapor pressure at high temperatures ensures minimal material loss.
 
 
 
• **Why Other Materials Are Not Suitable:**
 
 
• **Copper:** Low melting point (~1085°C) makes it unsuitable for high-temperature applications like filaments.
 
• **Aluminium:** Melts at approximately 660°C and lacks the durability required for filaments.
 
• **Iron:** Melting point (~1538°C) is higher than copper or aluminium but still insufficient compared to tungsten.
 
 
 
• **Inert Gas in Bulbs:** Modern electric bulbs are filled with inert gases like argon or a mixture of argon and nitrogen to prevent the oxidation of the tungsten filament and reduce evaporation.
 
• **Historical Background:** The use of tungsten in filaments was pioneered in the early 20th century, replacing earlier materials like carbon due to its superior properties.
 
• **Applications Beyond Bulbs:** Tungsten is also used in x-ray tubes, welding electrodes, and aerospace due to its heat-resistant properties.

• These plains are divided into three distinct sections: the **Konkan Coast** (Maharashtra and Goa), the **Kanara Coast** (Karnataka), and the **Malabar Coast** (Kerala).
 
• The region is known for its **fertile soil, lagoons, backwaters, and estuaries**, which support agriculture, fishing, and tourism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Western Ghats:**

 
 
• A UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the eight "hottest hotspots" of biological diversity globally.
 
• It is a continuous mountain range running parallel to the western coast of India.
 
• The Western Ghats play a crucial role in influencing the monsoon climate in India.
 
 
 
• **Arabian Sea:**
 
 
• Part of the northern Indian Ocean, bounded by India to the east, Pakistan and Iran to the north, and the Arabian Peninsula to the west.
 
• It is a major route for maritime trade and has significant economic importance.
 
 
 
• **Backwaters of Kerala:**
 
 
• A network of interconnected lakes, rivers, and canals along the Malabar Coast.
 
• Famous for houseboat tourism and traditional fishing practices.
 
 
 
• **Economic Significance:**
 
 
• The Western Coastal Plains are important for agriculture, with crops like rice and coconut grown extensively.
 
• Fishing is a major occupation along the coast due to the proximity to the Arabian Sea.
 
• The region also supports industries like shipbuilding and tourism.

questions.question: Which ancient civilisations flourished in the Thar Desert area about 5000 years ago?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indus Valley Civilisation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indus Valley Civilisation, also known as Harappan Civilisation, existed approximately between 3300 BCE and 1300 BCE in the northwestern regions of South Asia.
 
• It flourished in areas of modern-day Pakistan and northwest India, including the Thar Desert region.
 
• Major sites of the civilisation include Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro, Dholavira, and Kalibangan, which are all located near river systems and arid regions like the Thar Desert.
 
• The civilisation is noted for its advanced urban planning, including the use of baked bricks, drainage systems, and water storage facilities.
 
• It was one of the world's earliest urban civilisations alongside Mesopotamia and Ancient Egypt.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Terminology:** The term "Indus Valley Civilisation" is derived from the Indus River, around which many of the settlements were concentrated.
 
• **Key Features:** The civilisation was known for its trade networks, craft production, and script, though the script remains undeciphered.
 
• **Climate Context:** The Thar Desert region played a role in the civilisation's adaptation strategies, including water management and agriculture in semi-arid zones.
 
• **Decline:** The decline of the civilisation is attributed to environmental changes, such as the drying up of the Sarasvati River and possible shifts in monsoon patterns.
 
• **Archaeological Evidence:** Excavations have revealed seals, pottery, jewellery, and tools that provide insights into the daily life and culture of the Indus Valley people.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an elected position under the Panchayati Raj system in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Panchayat Secretary**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Panchayat Secretary** is not an elected position under the Panchayati Raj system; it is an appointed administrative role.
 
• The Panchayat Secretary is usually appointed by the **state government** to assist in the functioning and administration of the Panchayat.
 
• This role primarily involves record-keeping, maintaining accounts, and implementing government schemes at the Panchayat level.
 
• In contrast, positions like **Sarpanch, Zila Pramukh, and Pradhan** are elected by the people under the democratic framework of the Panchayati Raj system.
 
• The Panchayat Secretary acts as a link between the elected representatives and the state government for administrative purposes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Panchayati Raj System**

 
 
• The Panchayati Raj is a three-tier system of local self-governance in India, consisting of Gram Panchayat (village level), Block Samiti (block level), and Zila Parishad (district level).
 
• It was introduced through the **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992**.
 
• The system aims to empower rural areas with self-governance and decentralized administration.
 
• Each tier has elected representatives, ensuring grassroots democracy.
 
 
 
• **Key Elected Positions in Panchayati Raj**
 
 
• **Sarpanch:** Head of the Gram Panchayat, elected by the villagers.
 
• **Pradhan:** Chairperson of the Panchayat Samiti at the block level.
 
• **Zila Pramukh:** Head of the Zila Parishad, elected by the members of the Parishad.
 
 
 
• **Roles of Panchayat Secretary**
 
 
• Maintains records of meetings, resolutions, and accounts.
 
• Coordinates the implementation of government schemes and programs.
 
• Acts as a liaison between the Panchayat and state or district administration.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Panchayati Raj**
 
 
• Promotes participatory governance and decision-making at the grassroots level.
 
• Ensures the delivery of basic services like water supply, sanitation, and rural development schemes.
 
• Empowers marginalized groups, including women and Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes, through mandatory reservation of seats.

questions.question: Where was the 2024 G20 Summit held?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• The G20 is an international forum consisting of **19 countries and the European Union**, focusing on global economic issues.
 
• Rio de Janeiro, a prominent city in Brazil, is renowned for hosting international events such as the **2016 Summer Olympics** and the **UN Earth Summit (1992)**.
 
• The G20 Summit's agenda includes discussions on **sustainable development, global financial stability, and climate change**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **G20 Formation:**

 
 
• The G20 was established in **1999** in response to the financial crises of the late 1990s.
 
• It serves as a platform for the world's major economies to discuss and coordinate policies on international economic matters.
 
 
 
• **Members:**
 
 
• The G20 comprises **19 individual countries** (including the USA, China, India, Brazil, etc.) and the **European Union**.
 
• Collectively, G20 economies represent approximately **85% of global GDP** and **75% of international trade**.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Brazil:**
 
 
• Brazil has been a member of the G20 since its inception and plays a significant role in representing **emerging economies**.
 
• Its presidency in 2024 is expected to focus on **Amazon rainforest preservation** and **climate resilience**.
 
 
 
• **Previous Summits:**
 
 
• The **2022 G20 Summit** was held in Bali, Indonesia, and focused on global health and economic recovery post-COVID-19.
 
• The **2023 G20 Summit** hosted by India highlighted themes of **One Earth, One Family, One Future**.

questions.question: When you reuse slides from another presentation in MS PowerPoint 365, which of the following options ensures the imported slides retain their original formatting?

options.text: Import slides as images to lock their look
Apply the destination theme after inserting
Click 'Keep Source Formatting' in the Reuse Slides pane

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Click 'Keep Source Formatting' in the Reuse Slides pane**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• To retain the original formatting of slides when importing them into another presentation, use the **'Keep Source Formatting'** option in the Reuse Slides pane.
 
• This option ensures that the design, fonts, colors, and layout of the imported slides are preserved exactly as they were in the original presentation.
 
• It is a useful feature when you want to maintain consistency in the appearance of slides from multiple presentations.
 
• The Reuse Slides pane in MS PowerPoint 365 allows you to browse and insert slides from other presentations conveniently.
 
• By default, PowerPoint applies the destination theme to imported slides unless the 'Keep Source Formatting' option is selected.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Reuse Slides Pane:**

 
 
• Located under the 'Home' tab in the 'Slides' group, it allows users to insert slides from other presentations.
 
• Provides options to either apply the destination theme or retain the source formatting.
 
 
 
• **Source Formatting:**
 
 
• Refers to the original design and formatting of the slides in their source presentation.
 
• Includes design elements such as fonts, colors, background styles, and layouts.
 
 
 
• **Destination Theme:**
 
 
• This is the design and formatting of the presentation into which the slides are being imported.
 
• By default, PowerPoint applies the destination theme to ensure consistency within the current presentation.
 
 
 
• **Steps to Use 'Keep Source Formatting':**
 
 
• Go to the 'Home' tab and click on 'Reuse Slides' in the 'Slides' group.
 
• Browse to the source presentation and select the slides to import.
 
• Check the 'Keep Source Formatting' checkbox at the bottom of the Reuse Slides pane before inserting the slides.
 
 
 
• **Compatibility:**
 
 
• The 'Keep Source Formatting' feature is available in Microsoft PowerPoint 365 and other recent versions of PowerPoint.

questions.question: Which of the following is a disproportionation reaction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cl2 + H2O → HCI + HOCI**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Disproportionation reactions involve the simultaneous oxidation and reduction of the same species within a chemical reaction.
 
• In the reaction **Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl**, chlorine (Cl₂) undergoes disproportionation as it is both oxidized to form hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and reduced to form hydrochloric acid (HCl).
 
• The oxidation state of chlorine in Cl₂ is 0. In HCl, it is reduced to -1, and in HOCl, it is oxidized to +1.
 
• This reaction occurs naturally in water when chlorine is dissolved, and is often used in water purification and disinfection processes.
 
• Disproportionation reactions are a subset of redox reactions and are characterized by the same element undergoing both gain and loss of electrons.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Oxidation:** It refers to the loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation state during a chemical reaction.
 
• **Reduction:** Reduction is the gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation state during a chemical reaction.
 
• **Oxidation State:** It is a number assigned to an element in a compound or ion that represents the number of electrons lost (positive oxidation state) or gained (negative oxidation state).
 
• **Redox Reactions:** These are reactions in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously, involving the transfer of electrons between species.
 
• **Applications of Disproportionation Reactions:** Such reactions are widely used in industrial processes, water treatment, and chemical synthesis (e.g., the production of bleaching agents and disinfectants).

183:T1

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides a right to profess, practice and propagate religion?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 25**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 25** of the Indian Constitution guarantees all individuals the freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion.
 
• This article is part of the **Fundamental Rights** under Part III of the Constitution, specifically ensuring religious freedom.
 
• The rights under Article 25 are subject to public order, morality, and health, and other provisions of Part III.
 
• It applies equally to all persons, irrespective of their religion, ensuring secularism as a core principle of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Article 25 also allows the state to regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political, or other secular activities associated with religious practices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 26:** Provides the right to manage religious affairs, allowing religious denominations to establish institutions for religious and charitable purposes.
 
• **Article 27:** Prohibits compelling any person to pay taxes for the promotion or maintenance of any religion or religious institutions.
 
• **Article 28:** Addresses freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions.
 
• **Secularism in India:** Indian secularism guarantees the state’s neutrality towards all religions while allowing freedom of religious practices.
 
• **Restrictions on Article 25:** The state can intervene to regulate practices that contradict public order, morality, or health, or for social welfare reforms such as the abolition of untouchability or sati.

questions.question: According to 2011 census of India, which of the following states/union territories was observed as absence of tribal population?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Punjab**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• As per the 2011 Census of India, Punjab was reported as the state with **no Scheduled Tribe (ST) population**.
 
• This is attributed to the fact that during the reorganization of states in 1966, **tribal areas in Punjab** were allocated to other regions such as Himachal Pradesh.
 
• In contrast, other states like Odisha, Maharashtra, and Kerala have **significant tribal populations**, with Odisha being one of the states with the highest tribal populations in India.
 
• The absence of Scheduled Tribes in Punjab is a unique demographic feature when compared to other Indian states and union territories.
 
• Scheduled Tribes (STs) are officially recognized groups under the Indian Constitution, entitled to specific affirmative actions and reservations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tribal Population in India:**

 
 
• India is home to 705 officially recognized Scheduled Tribes, which constitute around 8.6% of the total population (Census 2011).
 
• The tribal population is concentrated in states like Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and parts of the northeastern region.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Provisions for Scheduled Tribes:**
 
 
• Article 342 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to specify Scheduled Tribes in states and union territories.
 
• Tribal populations benefit from reservations in education, employment, and political representation under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Census of India 2011:**
 
 
• The 2011 Census provided detailed demographic data, including the distribution of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) across states and UTs.
 
• The tribal population was recorded as 10.43 crore, with the highest numbers in states like Madhya Pradesh and Odisha.
 
 
 
• **Punjab's Unique Demographics:**
 
 
• Punjab has a significant Sikh majority population, with other communities such as Hindus and Muslims comprising smaller proportions.
 
• The absence of Scheduled Tribes reflects historical and administrative factors, including state reorganization and geographical distribution.

questions.question: The famous building 'Qutub Minar' has been built under which style of architecture?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mamulek Style**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Qutub Minar is an iconic monument constructed under the **Mamulek (or Mamluk) style of architecture**, which is a part of the Delhi Sultanate architectural tradition.
 
• It was commissioned by **Qutb al-Din Aibak**, the founder of the Delhi Sultanate, in 1192, and later completed by his successors.
 
• This architectural style is characterized by the use of red sandstone, intricate carvings, and calligraphic inscriptions, often incorporating Islamic motifs and verses from the Quran.
 
• The Qutub Minar is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and stands at a height of **72.5 meters**, making it one of the tallest minarets in the world built of bricks.
 
• The Mamulek style of architecture often blended Islamic and indigenous Indian elements, creating a unique fusion evident in monuments like the Qutub Minar.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mamulek Architecture:**

 
 
• Also known as Mamluk architecture, it emerged during the reign of the Slave Dynasty (1206–1290) in India.
 
• It extensively used locally available materials like red sandstone while incorporating Islamic architectural features such as arches, domes, and minarets.
 
• Floral patterns, arabesques, and geometric designs were a hallmark of this style.
 
 
 
• **Qutub Minar Construction:**
 
 
• Qutb al-Din Aibak began its construction, but it was completed by his successor, Iltutmish.
 
• It is surrounded by several historically significant structures, including the Iron Pillar and Alai Darwaza.
 
• The minar has five distinct storeys, each marked by projecting balconies and intricate carvings.
 
 
 
• **Delhi Sultanate Architecture:**
 
 
• It refers to the architectural developments during the rule of the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526).
 
• It includes other notable structures like the Alai Darwaza, the tomb of Iltutmish, and the Tughlaqabad Fort.
 
• This style laid the foundation for later Mughal architecture.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Site:**
 
 
• The Qutub Minar complex was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.
 
• It is recognized for its historical, architectural, and cultural significance.

questions.question:
Which of the following is/are correct with respect to the outcomes of globalisation in the Indian economy?

1. The opening of the economy has led to a rapid decrease in foreign direct investment and foreign exchange reserves.

2. The post-1991 India witnessed a steep decline in its GDP on a continual basis for two decades.

3. The growth of GDP increased from 5.6% during 1980-91 to 8.2% during 2007-12.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Globalisation in India post-1991 brought significant changes to the Indian economy, particularly through economic liberalisation policies.
 
• Contrary to statement 1, the opening of the economy led to a **rapid increase in foreign direct investment (FDI)** and a substantial rise in foreign exchange reserves.
 
• Statement 2 is incorrect as post-1991 reforms resulted in **economic growth**. The GDP growth rate did not witness a decline but rather showed improvement over time.
 
• Statement 3 is correct, as the growth rate of GDP increased from **5.6% during 1980-91 to 8.2% during 2007-12**, reflecting the positive impact of globalisation on economic growth.
 
• The correct answer is Option 2, as only statement 3 accurately reflects the outcomes of globalisation in the Indian economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Globalisation:**

 
 
• Globalisation refers to the process of integration and interdependence of economies, societies, and cultures through cross-border trade, investment, and technology.
 
• It promotes free flow of goods, services, capital, and labour across international borders.
 
 
 
• **Economic Reforms of 1991:**
 
 
• India introduced economic reforms in 1991, focusing on liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation (LPG model).
 
• These reforms aimed to address the balance of payment crisis and stimulate economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI):**
 
 
• FDI refers to investments made by foreign entities in the productive capacity of another country.
 
• FDI inflows increased significantly in India post-1991 due to liberalised policies and the removal of trade barriers.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Exchange Reserves:**
 
 
• India’s foreign exchange reserves increased from $5.8 billion in 1991 to over $600 billion in recent years, showcasing the positive impact of globalisation.
 
 
 
• **GDP Growth Trends:**
 
 
• India’s GDP growth witnessed a steady rise post-1991 reforms, with significant contributions from sectors like IT, manufacturing, and services.
 
• Improved infrastructure, policy reforms, and increased trade partnerships played a key role in sustaining high GDP growth rates.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states about the duty of Union Public Service Commission to present its report annually to the President of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is ​__**Article 323**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 323** of the Indian Constitution describes the duty of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to present its annual report to the President of India.
 
• The President places this report before both Houses of Parliament, along with a memorandum explaining cases where the Commission's advice was not accepted.
 
• This provision ensures the accountability and transparency of the UPSC's functioning.
 
• The Union Public Service Commission is a constitutional body established under Part XIV of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)**

 
 
• It is responsible for conducting examinations for appointments to civil services and posts under the Union Government.
 
• UPSC is one of the central recruiting agencies of India, established under Article 315 of the Constitution.
 
• The Commission consists of a chairman and other members appointed by the President of India.
 
• It functions independently to ensure unbiased recruitment for civil service positions.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Articles Related to UPSC**
 
 
• **Article 315:** Establishment of Public Service Commissions for the Union and States.
 
• **Article 316:** Appointment and term of office of members of the UPSC.
 
• **Article 317:** Removal and suspension of members of Public Service Commissions.
 
• **Article 323:** Reports of the UPSC and their presentation to the President.
 
 
 
• **Role of UPSC**
 
 
• Conducting examinations such as the Civil Services Examination (CSE), Engineering Services Examination (ESE), and others.
 
• Advising the government on matters related to recruitment, promotions, and disciplinary actions.
 
• Ensuring merit-based selection for appointments in public services.
